sections.h2: Which offices touch a Marion County deed
sections.html:
Three county offices handle every Marion County deed, always in the same sequence: engineer, auditor, recorder. The recorder comes last and is the one that places the deed in the permanent public record. You can reach the recorder at 740-223-4100, the auditor at 740-223-4020 and the engineer at 740-223-4110.

Beyond deeds, the recorder files mortgages, easements and related land papers. An online records system lets anyone look up property documents. Paper copies and certified copies require a visit in person or a written request with payment enclosed. The online system warns users to read the actual document, because database entries can be changed without notice.

sections.h2: What each office does with the deed
sections.html:
The order differs from counties that send the deed to the auditor first.

  • Engineer. Staff compare the deed's legal description with the engineer's records and stamp it approved. That stamp expires after 60 days, so a deed left sitting must be stamped again.
  • Auditor. The seller completes and signs a conveyance form. Payment has to arrive before processing begins, and the auditor then stamps the deed as transferred.
  • Recorder. The office confirms the deed was signed and acknowledged correctly and carries both earlier stamps. After recording, the original is kept for imaging and data entry and then mailed back or picked up.

Several other papers follow the same route: a certificate of transfer, an affidavit of survivor, a life estate, a transfer on death designation and a land contract. Putting the engineer first means a faulty description is caught before any money is paid to the auditor.

sections.h2: Fees at the engineer, auditor and recorder
sections.html:
The auditor's conveyance charge is a local rate, and the recorder's charge follows state law. Senate Bill 94 added $5.00 to recording fees for most documents.

Marion County deed steps and rates by office
OfficeStep or rate
EngineerApproval stamp on the legal description, valid 60 days
Auditor, conveyance$4.00 per $1,000 of the sale price
Auditor, line fee50 cents per parcel in the transfer
Auditor, very small sale$4.00 minimum conveyance fee plus line fees under a $1,000 price
Recorder$34.00 covers two pages, $8.00 each later page, plus the $5.00 surcharge

The auditor's online fee calculator asks for the total price, rounded up to the next dollar, and the parcel count. A box marks transfers that qualify as exempt on state form DTE 100 EX. Let the auditor confirm the final total before you write a check.

sections.h2: Sending a deed through the mail
sections.html:
You can, provided the stamps come first. No deed is accepted by mail unless it already bears current engineer and auditor stamps. The county describes three mailings:

  • The deed alone goes to the engineer, with a stamped, self-addressed return envelope
  • The approved deed then goes to the auditor with a signed conveyance form, a check and another return envelope
  • The twice-stamped deed finishes at the recorder with the recording fee

Expect the recorder to take about five days. That window covers proofing, imaging, and a side-by-side comparison of the image against the original before the deed goes back in the envelope you provided. Electronic filing skips the mail altogether. Four companies handle it: CSC at 855-200-1150, ePN at 888-325-3365, Simplifile at 800-460-5657 and Indecomm at 651-765-6400.

sections.h2: Closed days and your closing date
sections.html:
The recorder's closure list goes beyond the usual holidays. It has included Good Friday, Juneteenth, parts of the days around the Fourth of July, most of Thanksgiving week, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. In September the office has closed for the Popcorn Festival because of parking.

A deed cannot be recorded on a closed day. A buyer's lender sometimes wants proof of recording before releasing funds, so ask the title company which date it plans to file, and plan around the office calendar when the target falls near a holiday.

Marion County sits in the middle of Ohio, and the city of Marion holds the seat and the largest population. The 2025 estimate is 65,115 people, close to the 65,359 counted in 2020. Owners live in 67.5 percent of occupied homes. A typical owned home is worth $156,800, typical monthly gross rent is $864, and typical household income is $59,371. Of 27,348 housing units in 2020, 8.8 percent stood empty. Only 60 building permits were issued in 2025, so existing houses make up most of the sales.

The recorder's home page carries two warnings, a property fraud alert and a notary fraud alert, each linking to details. The Documents and Forms page holds three items: a public records policy, security procedures for electronic recording, and a notice to Medicaid Estate Recovery of a pending transfer of property by transfer on death deed.

That last notice concerns transfer on death deeds. Ask the office whether it applies before you plan a transfer of that kind. Staff cannot give legal advice and some questions may need an in-person visit, so bring the deed and any prior recording references.

sections.h2: Property taxes and a Marion County sale
sections.html:
Call the County Treasurer at 740-223-4030, the office that takes every property tax payment. The rate on a bill is the sum of voted levies and bond issues, and Ohio limits unvoted taxation to 10 mills, which works out to $10 per $1,000 of assessed value. Whatever exceeds that was approved by county voters.

The auditor's property search site accepts payments: look up the parcel by number, owner or address, open the tax tab on the property record, and add the amount due to your online cart, where you can adjust it before checkout. Debit and credit cards incur a 2.5 percent fee with a $1.50 floor, e-checks cost a flat $1.50 up to $10,000, and the page shows the amount before you submit.

For a seller, the practical step is to request a balance from the treasurer ahead of closing, so the title company can pay anything owed out of the proceeds and the buyer receives a clean record.

Steps for a typical sale

Have the deed drafted, then carry it to the engineer for the legal description stamp. Take the stamped deed to the auditor with the conveyance form and payment, and finish at the recorder with the recording fee. The engineer's stamp lasts 60 days, so do not stamp the deed until the closing date is firm. If the sale has no lender, there is no mortgage release to chase, and the three stops are all that stand between signing and the public record.

When you want proof for the buyer's lender, ask the title company to confirm the recording date once the original comes back. If you file by mail, keep the return envelopes handy and put a daytime phone number on each package. Call the recorder at 740-223-4100 if a package has not come back after about five days, and ask what stage it has reached.

faqs.q: What number reaches the Marion County Recorder?
faqs.a: 740-223-4100. The engineer's line is 740-223-4110 and the auditor's is 740-223-4020.

faqs.q: How many days does the engineer's stamp last?
faqs.a: Sixty. A deed that waits longer needs a fresh stamp before the auditor and recorder will take it.

faqs.q: What does the Marion County auditor charge on a sale?
faqs.a: The county charges $4.00 per $1,000 of sale price plus 50 cents per parcel. A non-exempt sale under $1,000 pays a $4.00 minimum plus the line fee.

faqs.q: How quickly does the recorder send a deed back?
faqs.a: Plan on about five days. That time covers proofing and imaging before the original goes back to you.

faqs.q: Is electronic recording available in Marion County?
faqs.a: Yes. CSC, ePN, Simplifile and Indecomm are the e-filing companies you can contact.
